chunks: He said: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, may God have mercy on him, reported to me that his father said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, from Muhammad ibn Ajlan, from Abu Abdillah Ja’far ibn Muhammad, peace be upon them both, who said:
Blessed is the one who does not exchange the blessing of God for ingratitude, and blessed are those who love each other for the sake of God.

الْمُتَحَابِّين.context: Derived from the root h-b-b (love), this reciprocal form denotes mutual love. ‘Loving for the sake of God’ (al-hubb fi Allah) is considered one of the highest virtues in Islamic ethics.

طُوبَى.context: An exclamation of felicity, often associated with the tree of Paradise (Tuba) in Islamic tradition, denoting supreme happiness for the righteous.

كُفْر.context: Here used in the sense of kufran al-ni’ma (ingratitude for blessings), a lesser sense of kufr distinct from outright apostasy, referring to failing to acknowledge and be thankful for God’s favours.

نِعْمَة.context: Refers to every form of divine favour — material, spiritual, and existential — that God bestows upon His servants.

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about gratitude for God’s blessings and loving one another for the sake of God?
ai.summary: Imam Ja’far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) pronounces a twofold beatitude: first for those who remain grateful for God’s blessings and do not repay them with denial, and second for those whose mutual love is rooted in devotion to God. The saying echoes the Quranic theme of Ibrahim 14:28, where those who exchanged God’s favour for ingratitude are condemned. In early Shi’a communities, cultivating bonds of love for God’s sake (al-hubb fi Allah) was regarded as one of the strongest manifestations of faith, strengthening communal solidarity among the believers.
